description:
Hi there! We are Team AUPET, competing in the  2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are passionate about technology, engineering, and space innovation, and we are tackling the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" challenge.
Our goal is to build a smart, user-friendly solution to help keep astronauts safe and healthy in deep space. We are looking for motivated teammates with skills in software and web development, coding!
summary:
SPACEVITALS is a decision-support dashboard for the crew medical officer on long-duration missions. On the way to Mars, Earth can be up to 22 minutes away, so health changes must be noticed and understood on board. SPACEVITALS compares every astronaut with their own baseline instead of population averages. It tracks vital signs with 7-day moving averages and z-scores, flags unusual multi-vital patterns with an Isolation Forest model, and explains every observation in plain language with a suggested next review step. It never gives a diagnosis.

Our focus is bone health, one of the best-documented risks of spaceflight: urine biomarkers (calcium, NTx, CTX) can show increased bone resorption early. An animated body map shows each organ system at a glance, the Radiation Monitor loads live NASA DONKI space-weather events, and a one-click report summarizes everything for the flight surgeon.

We tested our method on real data: applied to the blood chemistry of the four Inspiration4 crew members (NASA OSDR, OSD-575), personal baselines flagged 14 changes the day after landing, while standard lab ranges caught only 4. Crew data in the demo is simulated and labelled as such.
details:
THE PROBLEM

On a Mars mission, Earth is up to 22 minutes away and help is months away. Bone loss, cardiovascular changes and radiation exposure develop silently, and by the time symptoms appear, it is late. The crew medical officer needs to see problems early, on board, without waiting for Earth.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SPACEVITALS compares every astronaut with their own baseline: mission days 1-14 for vital signs, and pre-flight samples (L-60, L-30, L-7) for urine biomarkers. The analysis runs in three layers:

1. A 7-day moving average smooths day-to-day noise.

2. A z-score against the personal baseline raises Attention (2 SD or more) or Critical (3 SD or more).

3. An Isolation Forest model (unsupervised machine learning, 200 trees) looks at six vital signs together and flags unusual combinations that single thresholds miss.

Bone markers are checked against percentage rules (calcium +20/40%, NTx and CTX +30/60%). These thresholds sit inside the range NASA studies report for spaceflight (bone resorption about 50% higher in flight, collagen cross-links up to twice the pre-flight level). A combined observation fires when several markers rise together.

To prevent alert fatigue, three safeguards are built into the code: a vital-sign alert needs the 7-day average to stay beyond 2 SD for 3 consecutive days; it can reach Critical only when a second independent signal agrees (another vital sign or Isolation Forest); and a bone marker reaches Critical only when a repeat test confirms it. A "Top priority today" line shows the single most important issue and the next step.

Every observation states the baseline, the current value, the change, a plain-language explanation and a monitoring step. It never states a diagnosis or a treatment. The app has eight pages: Overview with an animated body map, Health Dashboard, Bone Health, Risk Analysis, Radiation Monitor, Medical Records, Crew Monitoring and Settings. A mission-day slider replays the mission from day 1 to day 120.

METHOD CHECK ON REAL NASA DATA

We applied the same personal-baseline method to the real serum chemistry of the four Inspiration4 crew members (NASA OSDR OSD-575, 14 analytes). The day after landing it flagged 14 changes, 10 of which were still inside standard lab reference ranges. The method also flagged 12 values six months after flight, which shows that three pre-flight samples underestimate natural variation. This result shaped our safeguards and our roadmap.

NASA DATA

The Radiation Monitor loads live space-weather events (solar flares, CMEs, SEPs, geomagnetic storms) from NASA DONKI (CCMC) and is honest about the limits: these are events, not a personal dose. Real Inspiration4 serum chemistry from NASA OSDR (OSD-575) is the scientific reference and the basis of our method check. The dosimeter scale is anchored to MSL/RAD cruise measurements (about 1.84 mSv/day), and the 600 mSv career limit from NASA-STD-3001 is shown for context.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SPACEVITALS turns raw numbers into early, explainable warnings, so countermeasures (exercise, nutrition, retesting) can start sooner, and a single crew medical officer has less to watch. The same personal-baseline approach applies on Earth: polar and remote stations, submarines and rural telemedicine.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with hand-built SVG charts: no frameworks, no build step, works offline and opens from a single link.

- Isolation Forest implemented in JavaScript and cross-checked in Python with pandas and scikit-learn.

- Python standard library script for the real-data check on OSD-575.

- PostgreSQL schema ready for a planned FastAPI backend. Hosting: GitHub Pages.

- Development was assisted by Claude (Anthropic). The voiceover in the second half of the demo video was generated with TTSMaker.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Personal baselines instead of population averages, checked on a real NASA crew.

- Bone health as a primary signal, not an afterthought.

- An animated body map that shows the whole crew member at a glance.

- Transparent analysis: every flag shows its reason and its confirmation status.

- Strict data honesty: every value is labelled LIVE, SIMULATED or NASA OSDR.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Medical safety: decision support only, no diagnosis; urine markers show bone turnover, not bone density.

- Scientific honesty: OSD-575 has only 4 crew members on a 3-day flight and contains serum, not urine. The Isolation Forest threshold was selected on simulated data, and the demo anomaly was placed in the simulation to test the detector.

- We deliberately do not combine animal and human data or model the ECLSS water loop: we only show what we can validate.

- Offline operation, accessibility (reduced-motion option) and privacy: no real personal data.

FUTURE POTENTIAL

- Calibrate thresholds on long-duration ISS data through NASA's data request process.

- Test the alert logic in a ground analog such as HERA.

- Connect real wearables and on-board urine analysis.

- Learn each astronaut's patterns over several missions.

- Support Earth-independent medical operations for Artemis, Gateway and Mars.
